analysis.one_liner: Requires big meatpackers to publish cattle contract terms and buy a minimum share of cattle through open bidding.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to force meatpackers to disclose cattle contract terms and buy more cattle through open bidding never received a committee vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large meatpacking companies to file their cattle purchase contracts with the Agriculture Department, which would publish the terms, premiums, and discounts in a public library and monthly report. It also would have required the biggest packers to buy a set minimum percentage of cattle through open, negotiated bidding rather than private formula contracts, with fines up to $90,000 per week for violations. The goal is to give cattle ranchers better price information and more bargaining power when they sell their animals.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent cattle ranchers and feeders gain the most: they would see the contract terms, premiums, and discounts packers offer, and packers would have to buy a minimum share of cattle through open negotiated bidding instead of locking in supply with private formula contracts. That gives sellers a real alternative and a better sense of what their cattle are worth. Consumers could benefit indirectly if more competitive bidding leads to fairer cattle prices, though the link to retail meat prices is not direct.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a public library of cattle purchase contracts between packers and producers, including premium and discount schedules, contract duration, and how many cattle are committed, so a rancher can see what terms are actually available before negotiating.

Requires the Agriculture Department to divide the continental U.S. into 5 to 7 regions and set a mandatory minimum percentage of cattle each big packer must buy through open pricing mechanisms like negotiated sales or public trading platforms, with the initial floor based on 2020-2022 negotiated trade levels and capped at 50%.

Applies only to 'covered packers' that slaughtered 5% or more of the nation's fed cattle over the previous five years, so the rules target the handful of dominant companies rather than small processors.
Adds reporting requirements that would give producers faster and more detailed market data, including prior-day delivery schedules and daily average carcass weights.
Sets civil penalties of up to $90,000 per violation, with each week of a continuing violation counted separately, giving the rules real teeth.

analysis.who_pays: The large meatpacking companies (those slaughtering 5% or more of the nation's fed cattle) bear the costs: they must file detailed contract information with USDA, give up some of their current ability to buy most cattle under private formula contracts, and face fines up to $90,000 per week if they fall short of the mandatory minimum of negotiated purchases. Some of that cost could be passed through to consumers as slightly higher processing margins, though competitive bidding could also push prices toward ranchers.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory minimums could raise packers' costs and reduce their flexibility to secure steady supply through formula contracts, and some of that cost could be passed to consumers at the grocery store.

The one-size-fits-all regional minimums may fit poorly: the bill lets USDA set floors between the 2020-2022 negotiated average and 50%, but in regions where little negotiated trade happens, forced bidding could disrupt existing marketing arrangements that ranchers voluntarily signed up for.

Packers can remedy shortfalls in later periods, and USDA must do notice-and-comment rulemaking with a cost-benefit analysis before setting the minimums, so the actual bite depends heavily on how the agency writes the rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to ranchers are concrete and targeted at a real imbalance: four large packers buy the vast majority of fed cattle, and most of it moves under formula contracts tied to prices the packers themselves influence in thin cash markets. The main costs fall on those same packers in the form of compliance and reduced procurement control, with a possible but uncertain pass-through to meat prices. The bill was designed cautiously — penalties capped at $90,000 per week, minimums negotiated through rulemaking, and remedies for first-time shortfalls — so it trades some of its potential force for political and legal durability.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Agriculture Committee for the entire two-year Congress and never got a hearing mark-up or a vote, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Deb Fischer introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, with 22 cosponsors split evenly between 11 Republicans and 11 Democrats, including Chuck Grassley, Jon Tester, Ron Wyden, and Sherrod Brown.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day; no further action appears in the record.
The committee never reported the bill or scheduled a vote, and the full Senate never considered it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpacking companies that dominate cattle buying are better off, because they keep purchasing most cattle under private formula contracts with no public contract library and no mandatory share of open negotiated bidding.

for.name: Sen. Deb Fischer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan cosponsor list

for.name: 22 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors from both parties, including Chuck Grassley, Jon Tester, Ron Wyden, Sherrod Brown, John Thune, and Amy Klobuchar

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Debbie Stabenow (D-MI) with Sen. John Boozman (R-AR) as ranking member
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no markup, no vote, no report — leaving it to die in committee

against.name: Large meatpacking industry
against.role: The packers slaughtering most of the nation's fed cattle, represented by trade groups such as the North American Meat Institute
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory minimums and contract disclosure requirements that would constrain their formula purchasing, in public comments on similar cattle price legislation

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly bipartisan — 11 Republicans and 11 Democrats cosponsored — and the bill never reached a floor vote, so no party-line roll call ever occurred.

industries.industry: Large meatpackers (Tyson, JBS, Cargill, National Beef)
industries.note: The bill targets packers slaughtering 5% or more of the nation's fed cattle, requiring them to disclose contract terms and buy a minimum share of cattle through open negotiated bidding, with fines up to $90,000 per week. Their core advantage — buying most cattle under formula contracts priced off thin cash markets — would be directly reduced, which is why atransparent, competitive bidding market matters for the ranchers selling to them.

Producers would get a public library of packer contract terms and a guaranteed share of open-bid purchases, improving price discovery and their leverage at sale time. Smaller feeders who lack inside knowledge of packer contracts benefit most.
More competitive cattle bidding could support fairer prices over time, but packers could pass some compliance costs into meat prices. The effect on grocery prices is indirect and uncertain.
